scenes.title: Near Earth
scenes.description: Start with our home and its Moon. Touch a world to look closer.

spots.label: Earth
spots.alt: The blue Earth with white cloud swirls, Africa, and Antarctica in the Apollo 17 photograph.
spots.title: A rocky world covered in water.
body: Earth is the third planet from the Sun. Oceans cover about 71% of its surface. The white swirls are clouds, while the darker blue areas are water. Africa and Antarctica are visible in this photograph.
Earth is the only world where we have found life. Its atmosphere and liquid water help make the surface habitable. The cloud cover here belongs to the Apollo 17 photograph taken in 1972.

spots.label: The Moon
spots.alt: The cratered Moon with dark lava plains and bright rays spreading from Tycho near its lower edge.
spots.title: The dark patches are ancient lava plains.
body: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. The broad dark areas are hardened lava that filled old impact basins. Brighter highlands and rays from craters surround them.

The Moon orbits Earth at an average distance of about 384,400 kilometers. The gap in this scene is compressed. Galileo's image combines visible and near-infrared observations, so its colors are enhanced.

scenes.title: The Sun and the rocky planets
scenes.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, in order outward from the Sun.

spots.label: The Sun
spots.alt: The Sun's bright disk with small dark sunspots in a visible-light image from the Solar Dynamics Observatory.
spots.title: The star at the center.
body: The Sun's gravity holds the Solar System together. Deep in its core, hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium and release energy. That energy eventually reaches us as sunlight.
The dark marks in this visible-light image are sunspots, cooler regions of the photosphere. The image is a monochrome view of the Sun's visible surface. The Sun is the only star in our Solar System.

spots.label: Mercury
spots.alt: Gray Mercury with a heavily cratered surface and bright patches, photographed by MESSENGER.
spots.title: A small world with an 88-day year.
body: Mercury is the smallest planet and the nearest to the Sun. It completes an orbit in 88 Earth days. The scars across its rocky surface are impact craters.
Mercury has a very thin exosphere rather than a substantial atmosphere. With little gas to retain heat, its surface can reach about 430°C in daylight and fall to about −180°C at night.
spots.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Carnegie Institution of Washington · MESSENGER

spots.label: Venus
spots.alt: Venus wrapped in pale cream clouds with curved bands in a Mariner 10 image.
spots.title: The heat is trapped beneath the clouds.
body: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and is close to Earth in size. Its thick atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide, traps enough heat to make it the hottest planet. Surface temperatures reach about 467°C.

The pale globe shows clouds of sulfuric acid droplets, which hide the ground. Mariner 10's image combines orange and ultraviolet observations to show cloud structure. The surface cannot be seen in this view.
spots.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Mariner 10 · Image processing by Kevin M. Gill

spots.label: Back to Earth
spots.alt: Earth with its blue oceans and white clouds.

spots.label: Mars
spots.alt: Rust-colored Mars with dark markings and the long Valles Marineris canyon system across its face.
spots.title: The red comes from iron.
body: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. Iron minerals in its rocks and dust oxidize, giving it a rusty appearance. The long dark scar across this view is the Valles Marineris canyon system.
Mars has a thin atmosphere and a cold surface. Spacecraft have found evidence of rivers and lakes from a wetter past. Its two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, have irregular shapes.

scenes.title: The asteroid belt
scenes.description: Between Mars and Jupiter, rocky bodies orbit through mostly empty space.

spots.label: Ceres
spots.alt: Ceres with a gray cratered surface, part of its globe falling into shadow.
spots.title: A dwarf planet among the asteroids.
body: Ceres is the largest object in the main asteroid belt and is classified as a dwarf planet. It is about 940 kilometers across. Its rounded shape sets it apart from many of the smaller, irregular asteroids.
NASA's Dawn spacecraft reached Ceres in 2015 after visiting Vesta. The two worlds are shown together here for exploration. In space, the belt's objects are separated by enormous gaps.

spots.label: Vesta
spots.alt: Vesta's uneven gray body with large craters and ridges.
spots.title: An asteroid with layers inside.
body: Vesta is one of the largest bodies in the asteroid belt. Its interior separated into a crust, mantle, and core early in the Solar System's history, as material heated and melted.
Dawn orbited Vesta before traveling to Ceres. Some meteorites found on Earth came from Vesta, giving scientists samples to compare with the spacecraft's observations.

scenes.title: The giant planets
scenes.description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

spots.label: Jupiter
spots.alt: Jupiter's cream and brown cloud bands with the Great Red Spot near the lower left of the lit side.
spots.title: The largest planet wears bands of clouds.
body: Jupiter is the fifth planet and the largest in the Solar System. Its stripes are moving cloud bands in an atmosphere mostly made of hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is an enormous storm.
Jupiter has no solid surface like Earth's. Its atmosphere gives way to deeper layers of gas and liquid under increasing pressure. Four of its large moons are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.
spots.credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute · Cassini · True-color mosaic

spots.label: Saturn
spots.alt: Saturn's pale golden globe and broad tilted rings, photographed by Cassini.
spots.title: Each piece of the rings has its own orbit.
body: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. Its broad rings contain countless pieces of ice, with rock and dust mixed in. Each piece moves around the planet. The gaps separate different parts of the ring system.
Saturn is a gas giant with no solid surface to stand on. One trip around the Sun takes about 29 Earth years. Cassini photographed the planet and its rings during a mission that ended in 2017.

spots.label: Uranus
spots.alt: Pale blue-green Uranus in the 2024 reprocessing of Voyager 2 observations.
spots.title: A planet tilted onto its side.
body: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. Its rotation axis is tilted by about 98 degrees, so it travels around the Sun almost on its side. One orbit takes about 84 Earth years.

Uranus is an ice giant. Much of its interior is a hot, dense fluid containing water, methane, and ammonia. Methane in its atmosphere helps give the planet its blue-green appearance. This view uses the colors rebalanced in a 2024 study.
spots.credit: Patrick Irwin/University of Oxford/NASA · CC BY 4.0 · Lower-left view from the published comparison

spots.label: Neptune
spots.alt: Pale blue-green Neptune with subtle clouds in the 2024 reprocessing of Voyager 2 observations.
spots.title: The eighth planet takes 165 years to circle the Sun.
body: Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun. One orbit takes about 165 Earth years. Its atmosphere has strong winds and merges into deeper layers without a solid surface to stand on.

Neptune and Uranus are closer in color than many familiar pictures suggest. Earlier Neptune images were made more intensely blue to reveal clouds. The reprocessed view shown here gives a closer estimate of its natural appearance.
spots.credit: Patrick Irwin/University of Oxford/NASA · CC BY 4.0 · Lower-right view from the published comparison

scenes.title: Pale Blue Dot
scenes.description: From beyond Neptune’s orbit, look back toward home. Touch the tiny point to zoom in.
scenes.quote: Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us.

spots.label: Earth, from far away
spots.alt: An enlarged crop of the original Voyager 1 photograph: Earth is a tiny bright speck in a streak of scattered light.
spots.title: Our home from six billion kilometers.
body: Voyager 1 photographed Earth on 14 February 1990, from about six billion kilometers away. Our planet was smaller than a single camera pixel. This close view enlarges the original image; it cannot reveal continents or clouds.

Carl Sagan proposed the distant Earth portrait in 1981 as a member of the Voyager imaging team. The mission team later pointed the spacecraft’s camera platform back toward the planets. Voyager 1 was already beyond Neptune’s orbit. Voyager 2 was the spacecraft that flew past Neptune in 1989.
The bright streak is sunlight scattered inside the camera. Earth happens to lie within it. This is the original published photograph, rather than the version reprocessed in 2020.
spots.credit: NASA/JPL · Voyager 1 · Crop enlarged from the original 1990 photograph

spots.label: Carl Sagan
spots.alt: NASA’s portrait montage of Carl Sagan, wearing a blazer with his hands in his pockets, against a background of stars and planets.
spots.title: A scientist who helped us see our place in space.
body: Carl Sagan (1934–1996) was an American astronomer, planetary scientist, author, and science communicator. He joined Cornell University in 1968 and remained there until his death, serving as a professor of astronomy and space sciences and directing its Laboratory for Planetary Studies.

His research helped explain Venus’s extreme heat through the greenhouse effect, seasonal changes on Mars through windblown dust, and Titan’s reddish haze through complex organic molecules. He advised NASA and contributed to missions including Mariner, Viking, Voyager, and Galileo.

Sagan brought astronomy into living rooms through the television series Cosmos and its companion book in 1980. The Dragons of Eden won the 1978 Pulitzer Prize for general nonfiction. His novel Contact appeared in 1985.

In 1980 he co-founded The Planetary Society with Bruce Murray and Louis Friedman. He also led the committee that selected the contents of the Voyager Golden Record, a collection of sounds, music, and images carried by both spacecraft.

The distant Earth photograph was an idea he championed as part of Voyager’s imaging team. He later reflected on it in his 1994 book Pale Blue Dot, connecting the astronomical view with our shared life on Earth. This journey pairs the original photograph with a brief quotation from that book.

scenes.title: Small icy worlds
scenes.description: Pluto and Arrokoth belong to the Kuiper Belt. The comet is shown on a separate visit near the Sun.

spots.label: Pluto
spots.alt: Pluto's mottled tan surface with a pale heart-shaped region.
spots.title: A dwarf planet with mountains and glaciers.
body: Pluto belongs to the Kuiper Belt, the region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. It is a dwarf planet, and its surface has mountains of water ice, plains, and glaciers.
The pale heart-shaped region includes a plain covered in nitrogen ice. New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, showing a much more varied world than the distant point of light seen from Earth.

spots.label: Arrokoth
spots.alt: Arrokoth's two joined reddish lobes, one larger than the other, against black space.
spots.title: Two small worlds joined together.
body: Arrokoth is a small Kuiper Belt object with two connected lobes. Scientists think the lobes came together gently early in the Solar System's history.
New Horizons passed Arrokoth in 2019, after visiting Pluto. Small bodies like this preserve material from the formation of the planets. The Kuiper Belt is still part of the Solar System.
spots.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/SwRI · New Horizons · Color composite

spots.label: A comet near the Sun
spots.alt: Comet Hartley 2's irregular nucleus with jets emerging from its brighter end.
spots.title: Warming ice releases gas and dust.
body: Comets contain frozen gases, rock, and dust. When one approaches the Sun, warming material releases gas and carries dust away from the nucleus. This can form a coma and tails.
EPOXI photographed jets from comet Hartley 2 in 2010. The nucleus is shown close up here. This photograph was taken on a visit near the Sun, separate from the Kuiper Belt views in this scene.
